result.answer: {"answer": "No — 11 of the 100 held-out patients (11%) also appear in training, so the reported 86% aggregate held-out accuracy is not a valid unseen-patient estimate; a corrected unseen-patient score cannot be recovered from the aggregate alone (patient-level data is required), and the minimal valid rerun is to split by patient identifier before feature fitting, fit normalization on training records only, and evaluate held-out patients absent from training.", "explanation": "Source_1 defines generalization as performance on patients absent from training and states that the held-out set contains exactly 100 unique patients, with split assignment required by patient identifier before feature fitting. Source_2 reports that exactly 11 held-out patient identifiers also occur in training, that the remaining held-out patients do not occur in training, and that no per-patient predictions were retained. Source_3 reports an aggregate held-out accuracy of 86%, but also says feature normalization was fitted on the union of training and held-out records before the split and that only the aggregate score is available. Using source_1's denominator of 100 and source_2's overlap count of 11, contamination is 11/100 = 11%. Because 11 held-out patients were in training and preprocessing used held-out records, the 86% figure is not a clean unseen-patient estimate. The documents are complementary rather than conflicting: source_1 gives the protocol, source_2 gives the overlap audit, and source_3 gives the reported score and preprocessing leak; none supplies a corrected score. A corrected score cannot be derived from the aggregate alone because only the aggregate score is available and no per-patient predictions were retained.
